title: How to choose an AI consulting company
description: A buyer's checklist for hiring an AI consulting company: what to ask, how to test their claims, what the work should cost you in time, and red flags to avoid.
job: Pick an outside team to help you use AI, without paying for hype or for work you cannot check.
summary: An AI consulting company helps a business decide where AI will pay off, builds or sets up the tools, and trains staff. Quality varies a lot, and the term AI is partly a marketing word. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission warns that some products with AI claims may not work as advertised. So treat every claim as something to test. Choose on the evidence: work you can inspect, a plan with a clear test, and a contract that lets you leave.

example.input: A 60-person distributor wants help with AI. It has two years of order history and a support inbox, and it has not picked a goal.
example.output: A good first deliverable is a short written plan. It names one task, the data needed, the measure of success, how the result will be tested on past cases, and the cost to find out. It is not a promise of savings.

howToTest: Ask for the plan before the project. It should name one task, one measure of success and one test. If it says 'transform your business', ask again.
Ask what they would do with your own past data in the first two weeks, and how you would judge the result. Start with a small paid trial.
Ask for two customers you can call. Ask those customers what was delivered, what was late and what did not work.
Ask who will do the work. The team in the sales call may differ from the team on your project.
Ask what you own at the end: code, data, trained models and documents. Check you can run it without them.

buyVsBuild.buy: Hire an outside company when you lack AI skills in-house and the task is well defined. Pay for a small first phase with a clear test. Extend only if it passes.
buyVsBuild.build: Build in-house when the task is core to your business and you can hire or train. Even then, a short outside review of your plan can catch weak spots early.

watchOuts: Be careful of claims you cannot check. The FTC asks whether AI claims are exaggerated, and whether proof exists that AI does better than a simpler tool.
Be careful of any firm that does not ask about your data. AI work depends on your data being usable.
Be careful of long contracts with no early exit. Prefer short phases, each with a pass or fail test.
A tool built by someone else is still your responsibility if it fails. The FTC says you cannot blame a third-party developer or a 'black box'.

resources.name: FTC: Keep your AI claims in check
resources.what: A U.S. Federal Trade Commission business blog post. It lists questions the agency may ask about AI claims, including whether a product exaggerates what it can do and whether it uses AI at all.
